To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) Q-learning is guaranteed to achieve the optimal value function within a multiplicative factor of 2 after only O(1/epsilon) episodes of experience, and that (ii) the Q-learning algorithm is guaranteed to converge faster than the model-based approach in the limit of large numbers of episodes.

Q-learning is asymptotically optimal, that it converges to the optimal Q-function at a rate of O(1/n), that the optimal policy can be recovered from Q-learning after a time of O(n), and that indirect algorithms can converge at a rate of 1/(n log(n)) if a model is used to estimate the value of a state-action pair, and at a rate of only O(1/n) if the model is used to generate a policy that is then executed.
Q-learning and model based methods converge at the same rate, and the convergence rate is exponential in the number of states and actions, but polynomial in the size of each state's support.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: How fast does Q-learning converge, and what is the best way to use the data collected by Q-learning?
finite-sample performance guarantees for reinforcement learning algorithms, and with the comparison of Q-learning to model-based approaches.
